issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette: Luis Hernandez, a 70‑year‑old dentist who grew up in a tight‑knit Puerto Rican enclave in South Florida, still wakes with a knot in his chest when the distant echo of a gunshot reaches his ears. The memory that floods him is not just the flash of smoke or the shouts he heard that summer when a terrorist bomb detonated outside a nearby shopping center, but the feeling that everything he has built—his practice, his wife’s legacy, his community—could be ripped apart again. The day the attack happened, Luis was on the front counter of his clinic, a bright room with white coats and a humming HVAC system, when a group of uniformed police officers burst in, shouting instructions. The officers’ presence, the authoritative tone, and the abrupt clatter of a gunshot that was not the clinic’s own alarm, were all triggers that sent him spiraling into the nightmare he now recounts in therapy. The trauma’s imprint is so vivid that whenever Luis hears any sudden or loud noise—a siren, a child’s scream, a door slam—he immediately begins a cycle of rumination, self‑blame and avoidance. The thought that he could have done something differently, that he might have foreseen or prevented the attack, haunts him, driving him to carry a handgun on his belt into his practice, to avoid news broadcasts that mention terrorism or military conflict, and to stay on high alert. Each time a uniformed figure enters his office or a conversation about the military surface, the triggers ignite his internal alarm, and his mind automatically turns to the event. The triggers therefore not only spark the traumatic memory but also propel him toward these maladaptive strategies, forming a loop that feels inescapable. In the quiet moments of his day, Luis is often alone in the office, his office chair creaking beneath him, the overhead light flickering. He scans the room for exits, the familiar outline of the hallway that leads to the back door. Even the most mundane sound, the muffled hum of the dental unit, can feel like a potential threat. He watches his patients closely, noting their breathing patterns, looking for any sign that they might pose a danger. This heightened threat monitoring—every footstep, every exhaled breath—feeds back into his sense of danger, making ordinary interactions feel fraught. The sense of threat amplifies his fear of authority figures and military topics, so when a news anchor on television talks about the war in the Middle East, he abruptly turns off the TV and checks the clock, feeling his heart race. When the memory of that night returns, Luis is overwhelmed. He cannot put the frightening event into words; the details are locked behind a wall of images and sensations. The sounds of gunfire, the sight of the building trembling, the smell of burning—he relives them as if they are happening now. The memory floods his senses and forces him to stop mid‑conversation with a patient, to retreat to his office. This vivid, non‑verbal reliving not only triggers his threat perception but also causes him to retreat further, to engage in the very rumination and self‑blame that keep the trauma alive. The intrusive memory is both a product of and a catalyst for his maladaptive coping. It returns when he hears the clatter of a metal chair or the distant thump of a construction truck, and each time it does, his avoidance intensifies: he stops answering the phone, postpones the cleaning of his dental instruments, and starts to dread the next clinic day. Luis’s avoidance behaviors ripple into his daily functioning. The habit of carrying a handgun into his office has made patients uneasy; some have requested appointments at other practices, and the few who stay are often uneasy. The fear of hearing gunfire in the news has left him disconnected from his community, causing a sense of isolation. The rumination has sapped his joy in his work, turning the routine of filling cavities into a chore devoid of the satisfaction he once derived from helping patients. The loop of triggers, threat monitoring, and maladaptive strategies has tightened over the years, with each new trigger feeling like a reminder that the danger is still looming. It is this relentless, escalating cycle that brought Luis to the therapist’s office. He can no longer keep his practice running smoothly; patients are nervous, his own patience is frayed, and the sense of constant vigilance is exhausting. What he is most afraid of is losing the sense of control he once had over his own life—a control that the traumatic memory keeps stealing away. Yet, he also hopes to reclaim that control, to speak about the event without feeling overwhelmed, and to return to a life where he can enjoy the familiar hum of his clinic without the ghost of gunfire behind it.
